title: Coding Adventure: Chess
beats: Starts with simplest thing: draw the board with two loops and a parity check for light/dark squares
Pieces drawn; represent each as a number with 3 bits for type and 2 bits for colour; 64-length array as board
FEN introduced after the array exists; walks one tiny fen string by hand (7 empty then k), then 'you get the idea'
Drag and drop attempts fail, sneaks an illegal move in; motivates legal move generation as the first real challenge
Offsets for orthogonal and diagonal moves, precomputed squares-to-edge table; sliding piece loop with friendly block and capture stop
Spares detail on other pieces; reveals check is not yet handled, calls moves pseudo legal
Self-described gross approach: play each move, check if opponent can capture king; tests it; random opponent, self-play as joke
Humans use pattern recognition and prune most moves; computers will instead crunch millions; says why brute force is the right tool
Replaces filter with attack maps and pin lines for speed; mentions skipped trial-and-error
Perft test: recursive move counter with depth; 400 positions at 2 ply, about 120 million at 3 moves each; compare with known numbers
Tricky test position fails; compares per-move breakdown against Stockfish to trace castling and pin/en-passant bugs
Mentions neural nets and Monte Carlo as newer approaches but chooses old-school; defines evaluation as piece-value sum
Search function: same recursion as perft but evaluates leaves; negamax sign flip explained; checkmate negative infinity, stalemate zero
Small tree of three moves evaluated step by step to show least-worst choice
Alpha-beta pruning as garden shears on a branch; same result but faster; dependence on move order
Move ordering heuristics; same position timed: 1 s and 3.5M positions, then 0.25 s and 0.5M, then 25 ms and about 5000
Horizon problem: piece counts mislead when captures pending; quiescence search of captures only
King and two rooks endgame: computer shuffles; adds bonus for opponent king near edge and own king close; tested on several endgames
Hard pawn endgame needs deeper search; transpositions; zobrist hashing; honest risk of collisions accepted
Presenter plays black against the engine and loses, narrates its king path
Opening shuffle fixed with piece-square tables; opening book from grandmaster games for variety
Plays games vs the engine, mentions deadline exceeded
Iterative deepening: first horrified by redundant work, then reveals the payoff via move ordering; admits explanation may not make sense
Names two weaknesses (king safety, pawn structure); promises return

metrics.misconception: yes 26:11: 'redundant repeated searches must be wasteful' is stated as presenter's own initial horror then reversed
metrics.brute_force: yes 6:23: play-every-move-and-check-for-king-capture legal move filter, plus plain minimax before pruning (12:55)
metrics.examples: ~5 test positions growing from starting position, to a test position, then endgames (K+2R, K+Q vs pawn, pawn endgame); perft depths 2,3,4
metrics.ending: Admits engine still weak, names king safety and pawn structure, promises revisit

new_moves.name: oracle-comparison
new_moves.what: uses a trusted external system (Stockfish) to localise a bug by diffing breakdowns

new_moves.name: measure-each-fix
new_moves.what: same input timed before and after every optimisation to make gains concrete

new_moves.name: stated-horror
new_moves.what: presenter admits discomfort with a counterintuitive idea before revealing why it works

new_moves.name: stress-test-then-patch
new_moves.what: each weakness is exposed on a specific position, then fixed with a minimal tweak and the same position retried

theory: Build the dumbest working version, then repeatedly find a concrete position where it fails and patch with the smallest idea that fixes that position. The viewer meets pruning, quiescence, and iterative deepening as answers to failures they just watched, and numeric before/after timings make each idea's value undeniable.
velocity: Scene builder: keep a library of failing test cases per concept; each new idea is triggered by one
Orchestrator: sequence by failure, not by textbook order; the next concept is whichever flaw is currently visible
Evals: require a before/after number or visual for every optimisation claim
Voice: use stated-horror or honest doubt before counterintuitive results (iterative deepening)
Ghost hands: play the learner's position against the engine so they feel the loss before the fix
Learner model: expert-oracle comparison suits advanced learners; skip for beginners
quote: The easiest way I can think of for fixing this is a little gross
